title: Falling Squares
description:
# Falling Squares

Squares are dropped one by one onto the x-axis. Each entry `positions[i] = [left_i, sideLength_i]` gives the left x-coordinate and side length of the next square.

A square falls vertically until its bottom edge reaches the x-axis or lands on top of an earlier square. It lands on an earlier square only when their horizontal ranges overlap with positive width. If one square ends exactly where another begins, they only touch at an edge and do not stack.

After each drop, record the highest y-coordinate occupied by any square so far. Return the list of those running maximum heights.

## Example 1

**Input:** positions = [[1,2],[2,3],[6,1]]

**Output:** [2,5,5]

**Explanation:** The first square covers [1,3) and reaches height 2. The second covers [2,5), overlaps the first on [2,3), and lands at height 2 + 3 = 5. The third covers [6,7) and lands on the ground, so the running maximum remains 5.

## Example 2

**Input:** positions = [[100,100],[200,100]]

**Output:** [100,100]

**Explanation:** The first square covers [100,200) and the second covers [200,300). They touch only at x = 200, so the second square does not stack on the first.

## Constraints

* `1 <= positions.length <= 1000`
* `1 <= left_i <= 10^8`
* `1 <= sideLength_i <= 10^6`

solutions.name: Brute Force Interval Check
solutions.description:
## Approach

Store every square that has already landed as a half-open interval [left, right) together with its top height. For each new square, scan all previous intervals, find the maximum height among intervals with positive overlap, place the new square on that base, and append the running maximum.

## Key Insight

Two squares interact exactly when their half-open x-intervals overlap: oldLeft < right && left < oldRight. Edge touching has zero width and therefore must not stack.

## Complexity Analysis

For n drops, each square scans at most all earlier squares, so the time complexity is O(n^2). The stored intervals and answer list use O(n) space.

solutions.name: Coordinate-Compressed Block Repainting
solutions.description:
## Approach

Collect every left and right edge, sort them, and treat adjacent coordinates as elementary x-blocks. For each square, scan the covered blocks to find the base height, then repaint all covered blocks to the new top height.

## Key Insight

Compression preserves every possible change point of the skyline. Between two neighboring compressed coordinates, the height is uniform for future overlap queries.

## Complexity Analysis

There are at most 2n - 1 elementary blocks. Each drop may scan and repaint all blocks, giving O(n^2) time and O(n) space.

solutions.name: Coordinate Compression with Lazy Segment Tree
solutions.description:
## Approach

Compress all square boundaries, build a segment tree over elementary blocks, query the current maximum height over the square footprint, then assign that footprint to base + sideLength with lazy propagation.

## Key Insight

A falling square overwrites the visible height over its whole horizontal footprint. Segment-tree range maximum query gives the base; range assignment records the new flat top efficiently.

## Complexity Analysis

There are O(n) compressed blocks. Each square performs one range maximum query and one range assignment, so the total time is O(n log n) and the tree uses O(n) space.

solutions.name: Ordered Disjoint Intervals
solutions.description:
## Approach

Maintain a TreeMap of disjoint half-open intervals and their current heights. Before placing a square, split intervals at the square boundaries, scan the covered pieces for the base height, remove those pieces, and insert one flat interval for the new square.

## Key Insight

After splitting at both boundaries, every interval is either fully inside or fully outside the new square footprint. That makes deleting the covered pieces safe without damaging neighboring heights.

## Complexity Analysis

Each operation uses ordered-map lookups, but a square can cover many existing intervals. The worst-case total time is O(n^2 log n) and the map stores O(n) intervals.

solutions.name: Dynamic Segment Tree on Raw Coordinates
solutions.spaceComplexity: O(n log C) worst case, O(nodes touched) in practice
solutions.description:
## Approach

Build segment-tree nodes only when a query or update reaches that coordinate range. Use the original x-coordinates directly, query [left, right] for the base height, and lazily assign the new height over that raw interval.

## Key Insight

Coordinate compression is not required if the tree is sparse. The domain is huge, but each square touches only O(log C) nodes on the paths and covered ranges it needs.

## Complexity Analysis

Let C be the coordinate domain. Each drop performs a range query and update in O(log C), so total time is O(n log C). Allocated nodes are bounded by touched ranges, with worst-case O(n log C) space.
